newsitem.title: SPAIN: Clinton mulls new ideas to restart Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Clinton mulls new ideas to restart Mideast peace.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he was very concerned about the deadlock in the Middle East peace process and was working on new ideas to get it moving again.
"It is obvious that we're going to have to see some new specific actions taken in order to get this thing going again," Clinton told a news conference after a two-day NATO summit in Madrid.
"I'm very concerned about what's happening in the peace process. I'm very concerned about the growing tensions between the Palestinians and the Israelis," Clinton said.

Formal Israeli-PLO peace talks have been frozen since the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began building a Jewish housing project in traditionally Arab East Jerusalem in March, infuriating Palestinians.
In Jerusalem, a Palestinian spokesman said Israel's defence minister and a senior PLO official planned to meet on Wednesday under U.S. and Egyptian auspices to try to revive the talks.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai and Palestinian Minister of Planning and International Cooperation Nabil Shaath would meet at the residence of U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk with Egyptian Ambassador Mohammad Bassiouny also attending, he said.
"I have been working before I came here to come up with some ideas about how we can start this again," Clinton said in Madrid.
"I think it can be done, it is a question of will and risk -- calculated risk -- that's what the peace process in the Middle East has always been about, and we are working on it now," he added.
Clinton declined to say what he had in mind, saying that the less he disclosed the more likely he was to succeed.
But he said it was essential that Palestinian security cooperation with Israel -- which was also broken off in March -- should resume "to keep down the violence" in Palestinian areas.
Riots have flared repeatedly in recent weeks in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

As sponsor of the Middle East peace process, the United States has been urged by Arab states to intervene to get the talks back on track. But U.S. officials say this is basically the responsibility of Israel and the Palestinians.
Clinton is under domestic pressure from the powerful pro-Israel lobby not to force Israel into concessions, such as stopping the controversial housing project, which Netanyahu has vowed not to do.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has not visited the region once in almost six months in office, although her predecessor Warren Christopher made some 20 visits during his four-year tenure.
Instead she has sent special envoy Dennis Ross to the region, but his efforts and a parallel mediation bid by Egypt have yet to bear fruit.

PLO officials said Wednesday's meeting would focus on confidence-building measures, including operating a Palestinian airport in Gaza, building a seaport and a three-stage Israeli pullback from rural areas in the West Bank, agreed under interim peace deals.

Netanyahu has proposed moving straight into negotiations on a final peace settlement with the Palestinians rather than pursuing talks on implementing outstanding elements of interim accords signed since 1993.
But the PLO demands he first halt the housing project at Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa, in East Jerusalem before fully-fledged talks can resume.
